entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Inheritance of the Tribe of Judah - Joshua 15</title> <div sID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> Under the superintending providence of God, the inheritance which fell to the tribe of Judah by lot was in the southern part of Canaan, where Caleb had already received his inheritance, so that he was not separated from his tribe. The inheritance of Judah is first of all described according to its boundaries (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.1-Josh.15.12">Jos 15:1-12</reference>); then for the sake of completeness it is stated once more with regard to Caleb, that he received Kirjath-arba for his inheritance, and took possession of it by expelling the Anakites and conquering Debir (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.13-Josh.15.20">Jos 15:13-20</reference>); and after this a list is given of the towns in the different parts (vv. 21-63).<hi type="italic">Boundaries of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah</hi>. - Jos 15:1. Its situation in the land. “<hi type="italic">And there was</hi> (i.e., fell, or came out; cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1">Jos 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.1">Jos 19:1</reference>)<hi type="italic">the lot to the tribe of Judah according to its families to the frontier of Edom</hi> (see at Num 34:3), <hi type="italic">to the desert of Zin southward, against the extreme south</hi>” (lit. from the end or extremity of the south), i.e., its inheritance fell to it, so that it reached to the territory of Edom and the desert of Zin, in which Kadesh was situated (see at Num 13:21), on the extreme south of Canaan.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.2-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference> <hi type="italic">The southern boundary</hi>. This was also the southern boundary of the land of Israel generally, and coincided with the southern boundary of Canaan as described in Num 34:3-5. It went out “<hi type="italic">from the end of the salt sea, namely, from the tongue which turneth to the south</hi>,” i.e., from the southern point of the Dead Sea, which is now a salt marsh.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5">Jos 15:5</reference> “The eastern boundary was the salt sea to the end of the Jordan,” i.e., the Dead Sea, in all its length up to the point where the Jordan entered it.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.11">Jos 15:5-11</reference> <div eID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.11">Jos 15:5-11</reference> we have a description of the <hi type="italic">northern</hi> boundary, which is repeated in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.15-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:15-19</reference> as the southern boundary of Benjamin, though in the opposite direction, namely, from west to east. It started “<hi type="italic">from the tongue of the (salt) sea, the end (i.e., the mouth) of the Jordan, and went up to Beth-hagla</hi>,” - a border town between Judah and Benjamin, which was afterwards allotted to the latter (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.19">Jos 18:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.12">Jos 18:12</reference>), the present Ain Hajla, an hour and a quarter to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Riha</hi> (Jericho), and three-quarters of an hour from the Jordan (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.50.11">Gen 50:11</reference>, note), - “<hi type="italic">and went over to the north side of Beth-arabah</hi>,” a town in the desert of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.61">Jos 15:61</reference>), afterwards assigned to Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>), and called <hi type="italic">Ha-arabah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.18">Jos 18:18</reference>, about twenty or thirty minutes to the south-west of <hi type="italic">Ain Hajla</hi>, in a “level and barren steppe” (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, R. ii. p. 302), with which the name very well agrees (see also <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. pp. 268ff.). “<hi type="italic">And the border went up to the stone of Bohan, the son of Reuben</hi>.” The expression “went up” shows that the stone of <hi type="italic">Bohan</hi> must have been on higher ground, i.e., near the western mountains, though the opposite expression “went down” in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.17">Jos 18:17</reference> shows that it must have been by the side of the mountain, and not upon the top. According to <reference osisRef="Josh.18.18-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:18-19</reference>, the border went over from the stone of Bohan in an easterly direction “<hi type="italic">to the shoulder over against (Beth) Arabah northwards, and went down to </hi>(Beth)<hi type="italic">Arabah, and then went over to the shoulder of Beth-hagla northwards</hi>,” i.e., on the north side of the mountain ridge of Beth-arabah and Beth-hagla. This ridge is “the chain of hills or downs which runs from <hi type="italic">Kasr Hajla</hi> towards the south to the north side of the Dead Sea, and is called <hi type="italic">Katar Hhadije</hi>, i.e., a row of camels harnessed together.”

Jos 15:5 “The eastern boundary was the salt sea to the end of the Jordan,” i.e., the Dead Sea, in all its length up to the point where the Jordan entered it.  Jos 15:5-11 
 
 In Jos 15:5-11 we have a description of the northern boundary, which is repeated in Jos 18:15-19 as the southern boundary of Benjamin, though in the opposite direction, namely, from west to east. It started “from the tongue of the (salt) sea, the end (i.e., the mouth) of the Jordan, and went up to Beth-hagla,” - a border town between Judah and Benjamin, which was afterwards allotted to the latter (Jos 18:19, Jos 18:12), the present Ain Hajla, an hour and a quarter to the south-east of Riha (Jericho), and three-quarters of an hour from the Jordan (see at Gen 50:11, note), - “and went over to the north side of Beth-arabah,” a town in the desert of Judah (Jos 15:61), afterwards assigned to Benjamin (Jos 18:22), and called Ha-arabah in Jos 18:18, about twenty or thirty minutes to the south-west of Ain Hajla, in a “level and barren steppe” (Seetzen, R. ii. p. 302), with which the name very well agrees (see also Rob. Pal. ii. pp. 268ff.). “And the border went up to the stone of Bohan, the son of Reuben.” The expression “went up” shows that the stone of Bohan must have been on higher ground, i.e., near the western mountains, though the opposite expression “went down” in Jos 18:17 shows that it must have been by the side of the mountain, and not upon the top. According to Jos 18:18-19, the border went over from the stone of Bohan in an easterly direction “to the shoulder over against (Beth) Arabah northwards, and went down to (Beth)Arabah, and then went over to the shoulder of Beth-hagla northwards,” i.e., on the north side of the mountain ridge of Beth-arabah and Beth-hagla. This ridge is “the chain of hills or downs which runs from Kasr Hajla towards the south to the north side of the Dead Sea, and is called Katar Hhadije, i.e., a row of camels harnessed together.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.13-Josh.15.19">Jos 15:13-19</reference> <div eID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> The account of the conquest of the inheritance, which Caleb asked for and received before the lots were cast for the land (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.6-Josh.14.15">Jos 14:6-15</reference>), by the extermination of the Anakites from Hebron, and the capture of the fortified town of Debir, is repeated with very slight differences in Jdg 1:10-15, in the enumeration of the different conflicts in which the separate tribes engaged after the death of Joshua, in order to secure actual possession of the inheritance which had fallen to them by lot, and is neither copied from our book by the author of the book of Judges, nor taken from Judges by the author of Joshua; but both of them have drawn it from one common source, upon which the accounts of the conquest of Canaan contained in the book of Joshua are generally founded.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.13">Jos 15:13</reference> <div eID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> As an introduction to the account of the conquest of Hebron and Debir, the fact that they gave Caleb his portion among the sons of Judah, namely Hebron, is first of all repeated from Jos 14:13. נתן impers., they gave, i.e., Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.13">Jos 14:13</reference>). The words “<hi type="italic">according to the command of Jehovah to Joshua</hi>” are to be explained from <reference osisRef="Josh.14.9-Josh.14.12">Jos 14:9-12</reference>, according to which Jehovah had promised, in the hearing of Joshua, to give Caleb possession of the mountains of Hebron, even when they were at Kadesh (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.12">Jos 14:12</reference>). The “father of Anak” is the tribe father of the family of Anakites in Hebron, from whom this town received the name of <hi type="italic">Kirjath-arba</hi>; see at Num 13:22 and Gen 23:2.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">Jos 15:21-32</reference> <div eID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2881" type="x-p"/> The towns in the <hi type="italic">south land</hi>. - <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> (south-land) was the name given to the southernmost district of Canaan in its full extent, from the Arabah, at the southern end of the Dead Sea, right across to the coast of the Mediterranean, and from the southern border of Canaan, as described in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.2-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference>, as far north as Wady <hi type="italic">Sheriah</hi>, below Gaza, on the western side, and up to the mountains and desert of Judah on the east, stretching across the wadys of <hi type="italic">es Seba, Milh,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ehdeib</hi>, above which that part of Palestine commences where rain is more abundant, and to which, as we have already observed at Num 13:17, the <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> formed a kind of intermediate link between the fertile land and the desert. It was a line of steppe-land, with certain patches here and there that admitted of cultivation, but in which tracts of heath prevailed, for the most part covered with grass and bushes, where only grazing could be carried on with any success. The term which <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> employ for <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> is <hi type="italic">Daromas</hi>, but they carry it farther northwards than the Negeb of the Old Testament (see <hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, Pal. Ill. pp. 185ff). The numerous towns mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.32">Jos 15:21-32</reference> as standing in the <hi type="italic">Negeb</hi>, may none of them have been large or of any importance. In the list before us we find that, as a rule, several names are closely connected together by the copula vav, and in this way the whole may be divided into four separate groups of towns.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21-Josh.15.23">Jos 15:21-23</reference> <hi type="italic">First</hi> group of nine places. - Jos 15:21. The towns “<hi type="italic">from</hi>,” i.e., at “<hi type="italic">the end of the tribe-territory of Judah, towards the territory of Edom</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Kabzeel</hi>: the home of the hero Benaiah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>), probably identical with <hi type="italic">Jakabzeel</hi>, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.25">Neh 11:25</reference> in connection with <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, but has not been discovered. This also applies to <hi type="italic">Eder</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jagur</hi>.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33-Josh.15.47">Jos 15:33-47</reference> <div eID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> Towns in the <hi type="italic">lowland</hi> or <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>. - The lowland (<hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>), which is generally rendered ἡ πεδινή in the <hi type="italic">Sept.</hi>, rarely τὸ πεδιόν (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.7">Deu 1:7</reference>), but which is transferred as a proper name ἡ Σεφηλά in Oba 1:19; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jer 32:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.13">Jer 33:13</reference>, as well as in 1 Macc. 12:38, where even <hi type="italic">Luther</hi> has <hi type="italic">Sephela</hi>, is the name given to the land between the mountains of Judah and the Mediterranean Sea, - a broad plain of undulating appearance, intersected by heights and low ranges of hills, with fertile soil, in which corn fields alternate with meadows, gardens, and extensive olive groves. It is still tolerably well cultivated, and is covered with villages, which are situated for the most part upon the different hills. Towards the south, the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> was bounded by the Negeb  (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>); on the north, it reached to Ramleh and Lydda, or Diospolis, where the plain of Sharon began, - a plain which extended as far as Carmel, and was renowned for the beauty of its flowers. Towards the east the hills multiply and shape themselves into a hilly landscape, which forms the intermediate link between the mountains and the plain, and which is distinguished from the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> itself, in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">Jos 10:40</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.8">Jos 12:8</reference>, under the name of <hi type="italic">Ashedoth</hi>, or <hi type="italic">slopes</hi>, whereas here it is reckoned as forming part of the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>. This hilly tract is more thickly studded with villages than even the actual plain (See <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 363, and iii. p. 29.) The towns in the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi> are divided into four groups.  <reference osisRef="Josh.15.33-Josh.15.36">Jos 15:33-36</reference> <div eID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2884" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">first</hi> group contains the towns in the northern part of the hilly region or slopes, which are reckoned as forming part of the lowland: in all, fourteen towns. The most northerly part of this district was given up to the tribe of Dan on the second division (Jos 19:41.). <hi type="italic">Eshtaol</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zoreah</hi>, which were assigned to the tribe of Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.41">Jos 19:41</reference>), and were partly inhabited by Danites (Jdg 13:25; Jdg 18:2, Jdg 18:8,Jdg 18:11) and partly by families of Judah, who had gone out from Kirjath-jearim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.53">1Ch 1:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.2">1Ch 4:2</reference>), probably after the removal of the 600 Danites to Laish-Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.47">Jos 19:47</reference>; Jdg 18:1), were situated, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Esthaul</hi> and <hi type="italic">Saara</hi>), ten Roman miles to the north of Eleutheropolis, on the road to Nicopolis. <hi type="italic">Zoreah</hi>, the home of Samson, who was buried between Zoreah and Eshtaol (Jdg 13:2; Jdg 16:31), was fortified by Rehoboam, and still inhabited by Judaeans after the captivity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.10">2Ch 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.29">Neh 11:29</reference>); it has been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Surá</hi>, at the south-western end of the mountain range which bounds the Wady es Surar on the north (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 341, and Bibl. Res. p. 153). <hi type="italic">Eshtaol</hi> has probably been preserved in <hi type="italic">Um Eshteiyeh</hi>, to the south-west (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 342). <hi type="italic">Ashnah</hi> is possibly to be read <hi type="italic">Ashvah</hi>, according to the lxx, Cod. Vat. (Ἄσσα). In that case it might resemble a town on the east of Zorea (<hi type="italic">Tobler</hi>, p. 180), as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes.
entries.content_plain:
Jos 15:33-47 
 
 Towns in the lowland or shephelah. - The lowland (shephelah), which is generally rendered ἡ πεδινή in the Sept., rarely τὸ πεδιόν (Deu 1:7), but which is transferred as a proper name ἡ Σεφηλά in Oba 1:19; Jer 32:44; Jer 33:13, as well as in 1 Macc. 12:38, where even Luther has Sephela, is the name given to the land between the mountains of Judah and the Mediterranean Sea, - a broad plain of undulating appearance, intersected by heights and low ranges of hills, with fertile soil, in which corn fields alternate with meadows, gardens, and extensive olive groves. It is still tolerably well cultivated, and is covered with villages, which are situated for the most part upon the different hills. Towards the south, the shephelah was bounded by the Negeb  (Jos 15:21); on the north, it reached to Ramleh and Lydda, or Diospolis, where the plain of Sharon began, - a plain which extended as far as Carmel, and was renowned for the beauty of its flowers. Towards the east the hills multiply and shape themselves into a hilly landscape, which forms the intermediate link between the mountains and the plain, and which is distinguished from the shephelah itself, in Jos 10:40 and Jos 12:8, under the name of Ashedoth, or slopes, whereas here it is reckoned as forming part of the shephelah. This hilly tract is more thickly studded with villages than even the actual plain (See Rob. Pal. ii. p. 363, and iii. p. 29.) The towns in the shephelah are divided into four groups.  Jos 15:33-36 
 
 The first group contains the towns in the northern part of the hilly region or slopes, which are reckoned as forming part of the lowland: in all, fourteen towns. The most northerly part of this district was given up to the tribe of Dan on the second division (Jos 19:41.). Eshtaol and Zoreah, which were assigned to the tribe of Dan (Jos 19:41), and were partly inhabited by Danites (Jdg 13:25; Jdg 18:2, Jdg 18:8,Jdg 18:11) and partly by families of Judah, who had gone out from Kirjath-jearim (1Ch 1:53; 1Ch 4:2), probably after the removal of the 600 Danites to Laish-Dan (Jos 19:47; Jdg 18:1), were situated, according to the Onom. (s. v. Esthaul and Saara), ten Roman miles to the north of Eleutheropolis, on the road to Nicopolis. Zoreah, the home of Samson, who was buried between Zoreah and Eshtaol (Jdg 13:2; Jdg 16:31), was fortified by Rehoboam, and still inhabited by Judaeans after the captivity (2Ch 11:10; Neh 11:29); it has been preserved in the ruins of Surá, at the south-western end of the mountain range which bounds the Wady es Surar on the north (Rob. ii. p. 341, and Bibl. Res. p. 153). Eshtaol has probably been preserved in Um Eshteiyeh, to the south-west (Rob. ii. p. 342). Ashnah is possibly to be read Ashvah, according to the lxx, Cod. Vat. (Ἄσσα). In that case it might resemble a town on the east of Zorea (Tobler, p. 180), as Knobel supposes.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.61-Josh.15.62">Jos 15:61-62</reference> <div eID="gen2895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">towns in the desert of Judah</hi>, which ran along the Dead Sea from the northern border of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">Jos 15:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.7">Jos 15:7</reference>) to Wady Fikreh on the south, and reached to the districts of Maon, Ziph, Tekoah, and Bethlehem towards the west. This tract of land is for the most part a terrible desert, with a soil composed of chalk, marl, and limestone, and with bald mountains covered with flint and hornstone, and without the slightest trace of vegetation on the side bordering on the Dead Sea (see <hi type="italic">v. Schubert</hi>, Reise, iii. pp. 94, 96; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. pp. 202, 475, 477). Yet wherever there are springs even this desert is covered with a luxuriant vegetation, as far as the influence of the water extends (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. pp. 249, 258); and even in those parts which are now completely desolate, there are traces of the work of man of a very ancient date in all directions (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 187). Six towns are mentioned in the verses before us. <hi type="italic">Beth-arabah:</hi> see at Jos 15:6. <hi type="italic">Middin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Secaca</hi> are unknown. According to <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, <hi type="italic">Middin</hi> is probably the ruins of <hi type="italic">Mird</hi> or <hi type="italic">Mardeh</hi>, to the west of the northern end of the Dead Sea (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 270).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference> <div eID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2897" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference> there follows a notice to the effect that the Judaeans were unable to expel the Jebusites from Jerusalem, which points back to the time immediately after Joshua, when the Judaeans had taken Jerusalem and burned it (Jdg 1:8), but were still unable to maintain possession. This notice is not at variance with either <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference> or Jdg 1:21, since it neither affirms that Jerusalem belonged to the tribe of Judah, nor that Judah alone laid claim to the possession of the town to the exclusion of the Benjamites (see the explanation of Jdg 1:8).  <chapter eID="Josh.15"/> <div eID="gen2897" type="x-p"/>
